title: Agent Runtime Platform Engineer
tagline: Build the paved road that lets every team in the bank ship AI agents safely, without reinventing Kubernetes, identity, or MCP plumbing each time.
overview: This is not an 'AI engineer' role in the sense of building prompts or fine-tuning models — it is a platform engineering role where the product happens to be agent workloads. A bank like XYZ Bank needs this because every application team is suddenly trying to run LLM-backed agents and MCP servers, and without a shared runtime, each team will independently (and inconsistently) solve identity, secrets, networking, scaling, and observability — creating audit and security exposure at a regulated institution. Interviewers are probing for whether you think like an infrastructure/platform owner first (reusable modules, golden paths, self-service, guardrails) and only secondarily as someone who understands agent concepts (MCP, tool-calling, orchestration) well enough to design the runtime they need. A strong candidate frames every answer around 'how do I make this repeatable, secure, and self-service for 20 teams' rather than 'how do I build one agent that works.' Expect deep technical drill-down on AKS/Container Apps trade-offs, Kubernetes workload identity, Terraform module design, and secure MCP connectivity patterns, plus system-design and behavioral questions about driving adoption of a platform that teams don't have to use.

sections.heading: Choosing and Designing the Agent Runtime (AKS vs Container Apps vs Event-Driven)
sections.summary: Covers how to pick and combine AKS, Azure Container Apps, and queue/event infrastructure to host agents, MCP servers, and APIs — the foundational architecture decision this role owns.

content.text: Agent workloads at a bank fall into distinct runtime shapes: long-running conversational agents behind an API, short-lived tool-calling MCP servers, async batch/event-driven agents (e.g. reacting to a queue of transaction alerts), and scheduled/orchestrated multi-agent pipelines. Not all of these belong on the same compute platform, and picking the right one per workload — rather than defaulting to 'everything is a Kubernetes deployment' — is the core architectural judgment call this role makes daily.

rows: Abstraction level
Serverless containers on managed Kubernetes (KEDA + Dapr built in), no cluster to operate
Full Kubernetes API access — you own the cluster, nodes, CNI, and control plane config
Best fit for agents
Stateless MCP servers, tool endpoints, single-purpose agent APIs, queue-driven workers
Multi-tenant agent platforms needing custom operators, service mesh, GPU node pools, or colocated inference
Scaling
Scale-to-zero and KEDA-based event scaling out of the box
KEDA available but you configure it yourself; more control over bin-packing and node pools
Networking control
Internal environments, Dapr service invocation, simpler ingress
Full control over network policies, private endpoints, custom ingress controllers, service mesh (Istio/Linkerd)
Identity
Managed identity per container app
Workload Identity Federation via OIDC + Kubernetes service accounts, more granular per-namespace/per-pod
Operational overhead
Low — Microsoft manages the cluster
Higher — platform team owns upgrades, node image patching, cluster add-ons
When to avoid
GPU inference, custom Kubernetes operators, strict cluster-level compliance controls
Simple stateless APIs where cluster ops overhead isn't justified

content.text: A common enterprise pattern in 2026: MCP servers and lightweight agent tool-endpoints run on Azure Container Apps (fast to ship, scale-to-zero, Dapr sidecars for service-to-service calls), while the core multi-tenant agent orchestration platform — especially anything needing GPU node pools, custom admission controllers, or a service mesh for zero-trust east-west traffic — runs on AKS. Async and long-running agent work (document processing, batch reasoning, human-in-the-loop approval workflows) is driven off Azure Service Bus or Event Grid, with agents scaling via KEDA off queue depth rather than sitting idle as always-on pods.

items: Use Container Apps when the team needs to ship an MCP server or agent API fast and doesn't need cluster-level primitives
Use AKS when you need GPU pools for local inference, custom network policies, service mesh, or you're consolidating many teams' agent workloads under one platform-managed cluster
Use Service Bus/Event Grid + KEDA for bursty, async agent triggers (e.g. a document lands, an alert fires) so agents scale to zero between events
Co-locate MCP servers close to the agents that call them (same VNet, private endpoints) to avoid the latency and egress cost of round-tripping through the public internet

content.code:
# KEDA ScaledObject: scale an agent worker off Service Bus queue depth
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: claims-triage-agent
  namespace: agents-prod
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: claims-triage-agent-deployment
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 25
  cooldownPeriod: 120
  triggers:
    - type: azure-servicebus
      metadata:
        queueName: claims-agent-tasks
        namespace: sb-agents-prod
        messageCount: "5"
      authenticationRef:
        name: keda-trigger-auth-workload-identity

interviewQA.q: When would you put an MCP server on Azure Container Apps instead of AKS?
interviewQA.a: If it's a stateless, single-purpose tool endpoint — say, a server exposing three tools against a policy database — I'd default to Container Apps. It gives me scale-to-zero, KEDA-based event scaling, and managed identity without me having to operate a cluster, patch nodes, or manage ingress controllers. I'd only pull it onto AKS if it needed to share a network boundary or service mesh with other cluster-resident workloads, needed GPU access, or the team already had strong AKS operational maturity and wanted one control plane for everything. The decision is really about matching operational complexity to what the workload actually needs, not defaulting to Kubernetes because that's what we know.

interviewQA.q: How do you handle async, bursty agent workloads without paying for idle compute?
interviewQA.a: I drive them off events rather than keeping agents always-on. A message lands in Service Bus or an event fires in Event Grid, KEDA watches queue depth and scales the agent deployment from zero to N replicas, and once the queue drains it scales back down. This matters a lot at a bank where agent workloads like claims triage or transaction review are spiky — you don't want to provision for peak 24/7. I'd pair this with a dead-letter queue and a retry policy so a failing agent doesn't silently drop work, and with per-message idempotency since agents will occasionally reprocess a message.

interviewQA.q: How do MCP servers, agents, and the underlying LLM endpoint fit together in your runtime topology?
interviewQA.a: The agent runtime — whether that's a LangGraph graph or an Agent Framework orchestrator — calls out to an LLM endpoint via Azure AI Foundry or APIM's model gateway, and separately holds one or more MCP client connections, each to a dedicated MCP server that exposes tools, resources, or prompts. I keep those MCP servers as separate deployable units, not embedded in the agent process, so a policy-lookup MCP server can be reused across five different agents instead of five teams reimplementing the same tool integration. Network-wise I keep that traffic inside the VNet with private endpoints rather than letting agents call public MCP endpoints.

interviewQA.q: What's your view on running GPU inference alongside agent orchestration on the same cluster?
interviewQA.a: I'd separate them into different node pools at minimum, and often different clusters. Agent orchestration is typically CPU-bound, bursty, and needs fast scale-up/down, whereas GPU inference nodes are expensive, slow to provision, and benefit from being packed tightly. Mixing them risks the orchestration layer's scaling behavior fighting with GPU node pool constraints, and it also complicates cost attribution. I'd keep GPU-backed model hosting as its own AKS node pool or push it to a managed inference service, and let the agent runtime call it over the network like any other model endpoint.

interviewQA.q: How would you decide whether a new team's agent workload needs its own AKS cluster or can share the platform cluster?
interviewQA.a: Default to shared — most teams don't need cluster-level isolation, and multiplying clusters multiplies patching, upgrade, and cost overhead for the platform team. I'd isolate to a dedicated cluster only for hard regulatory boundaries — e.g. a workload subject to different data residency rules, or one where blast-radius requirements mean a noisy-neighbor incident can't be tolerated. Otherwise namespaces, network policies, resource quotas, and workload identity give you strong enough isolation on a shared cluster, and it's far cheaper to operate.

sections.heading: Platform Engineering Standards: Reusable Infra, Platform APIs, and Golden Paths
sections.summary: Covers how to build the reusable Terraform modules, platform APIs, and golden-path templates that let application teams provision agent infrastructure without recreating decisions — the essence of internal platform engineering.

content.text: The industry term for what this role builds is a 'golden path' or 'paved road' — a phrase Netflix and Spotify popularized and that's now standard platform-engineering vocabulary: a preconfigured, opinionated, end-to-end workflow that gets a team from zero to a production-ready, compliant workload fast, without them having to make (or get wrong) every infrastructure decision themselves. A mature golden path for agent workloads should take a team from 'we want to deploy an agent' to a running, observable, identity-scoped workload in AKS or Container Apps in well under a day, not weeks.

items: Reusable Terraform modules for: AKS node pools / Container Apps environments, workload identity + federated credentials, Key Vault + CSI driver wiring, APIM/ingress route registration, Service Bus namespaces and KEDA scalers

A platform API (or CLI/Backstage software template) that provisions a new agent workspace: namespace, service account, RBAC, network policy, secrets binding, and CI/CD pipeline — declaratively, from a short manifest

Environment-aware provisioning: the same module produces a smaller, less-isolated footprint in dev and a fully locked-down, HA footprint in prod, driven by environment variables/tfvars rather than forked code

Guardrails baked into the module, not left to reviewers: e.g. it is structurally impossible to provision a public ingress without going through the approved API gateway, because the module doesn't expose that as an option

rows: Infra module
Compute + networking baseline for an agent workload
Terraform module `agent-runtime-aca` / `agent-runtime-aks-ns`
Identity module
Workload identity + federated credential wiring
Terraform module `workload-identity-binding`
Platform API
Self-service provisioning without a ticket to the platform team
Backstage software template / internal CLI `agentctl new`
CI/CD template
Build, scan, sign, deploy pipeline reused across teams
GitHub Actions reusable workflow `agent-deploy.yml`
Policy-as-code
Guardrails enforced automatically, not by manual review
OPA/Conftest or Azure Policy on Terraform plans

content.code:
# Reusable Terraform module call — a team just fills this in, not the internals
module "agent_runtime" {
  source  = "app.terraform.io/adcb/agent-runtime-aca/azurerm"
  version = "~> 2.4"

  team            = "fraud-ops"
  environment     = "prod"
  agent_name      = "txn-review-agent"
  container_image = "acrbankprod.azurecr.io/agents/txn-review:1.4.0"

  key_vault_name        = "kv-agents-prod"
  workload_identity_ref = "txn-review-agent-sa"
  scale_rules = {
    min_replicas = 0
    max_replicas = 10
    queue_name   = "txn-review-tasks"
  }

  network_profile = "private-vnet-integration"
}

interviewQA.q: How do you design a Terraform module so it's actually reused instead of copy-pasted?
interviewQA.a: The main thing is keeping the interface small and opinionated — expose the handful of inputs a team genuinely needs to vary, like image, scaling limits, and team/namespace, and hide everything else, like network wiring and identity binding, inside the module. If I expose forty variables, teams will copy the module source and tweak it instead of consuming it as a dependency, and then I've lost my single point of control for security and compliance updates. I also version modules semantically and publish them through a private registry so teams pin versions deliberately, and I test modules with Terratest or similar so a breaking change is caught before it hits every consumer.

interviewQA.q: What does a 'golden path' actually look like for an agent workload here, concretely?
interviewQA.a: A developer runs something like `agentctl new --name txn-review-agent --team fraud-ops`, which scaffolds a repo from a template with the Dockerfile, MCP client config, CI pipeline, and a Terraform call already wired to our shared modules. They push, the pipeline builds, scans, and opens a PR against the infra repo with the plan output for review, and on merge it provisions a namespace with workload identity, Key Vault access, and APIM route already configured — all before they've written a line of custom infrastructure code. The whole point is that the 'boring' 80% — identity, secrets, network, logging — is solved once by the platform team and inherited by everyone else.

interviewQA.q: How do you keep golden paths from becoming rigid and blocking legitimate edge cases?
interviewQA.a: I treat the golden path as the default, not the only path — teams can go off-road, but going off-road means they take on the operational and security burden themselves, which is a deliberate disincentive, not a hard block. I also make sure there's a fast feedback loop for the platform team to add new capabilities to the paved road when enough teams need the same 'edge case,' so the road actually gets wider over time instead of everyone permanently detouring. And I version the templates so early adopters aren't stuck if we change direction.

interviewQA.q: Gartner data suggests most platform engineering initiatives fail to show impact. What would you actually measure to prove this platform is working?
interviewQA.a: I'd track time-to-first-deploy for a new agent team, the percentage of agent workloads actually on the golden path versus bespoke infra, incident rate and mean-time-to-recovery for platform-hosted workloads versus bespoke ones, and adoption trend over time rather than a single snapshot. The failure mode I've seen elsewhere is building a beautiful platform nobody uses because it wasn't co-designed with a real consuming team — so I'd also track qualitative developer satisfaction and treat low adoption as a signal to go talk to teams, not just a metrics problem to dashboard away.

interviewQA.q: How do you balance being a platform team versus becoming a bottleneck that every team has to route through?
interviewQA.a: Self-service is the antidote — if every provisioning request requires a platform engineer to click buttons, I've just recreated a ticket queue with extra steps. I aim for the platform team to build and own the modules and guardrails, but the actual provisioning happens through pipelines and APIs teams trigger themselves, with the platform team only in the loop for exceptions or new capability requests. That said, for a bank, some things — like anything touching customer PII or external network egress — legitimately need a human sign-off, so I'd build an approval gate into the pipeline for those specific cases rather than gatekeeping everything.

sections.heading: Agent Engineering Standards: Manifests, Runtime Config, and the MCP Protocol
sections.summary: Covers agent manifest design, tool/runtime configuration standards, and a protocol-level understanding of MCP — what interviewers use to check you actually understand what you're building a runtime for.

content.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the emerging standard for how agents discover and call tools, read context, and use reusable prompts — and as of the 2026-07-28 spec revision, its transport layer moved to a stateless model (no more Mcp-Session-Id header), meaning any server instance behind ordinary load-balanced HTTP infrastructure can answer a request, which matters directly for how you deploy MCP servers on AKS/Container Apps. The protocol splits into a data layer (JSON-RPC 2.0 messages defining discovery, capability negotiation, and the tools/resources/prompts primitives) and a transport layer (stdio for local subprocess communication, or Streamable HTTP for remote servers, with OAuth as the recommended auth mechanism). An MCP host is the application coordinating everything (e.g. the agent runtime), an MCP client is the 1:1 connection inside the host to a specific server, and an MCP server exposes the actual tools/resources/prompts.

items: Tools — callable functions the model can invoke, each described by name, description, and a JSON Schema input contract; this is the primitive platform teams should standardize hardest, since a badly-scoped tool is a security hole
Resources — read-only context identified by URI (files, DB records, API responses) that the host can attach to a conversation without the model 'calling' anything
Prompts — reusable, server-defined prompt templates that clients can surface to users or inject into a conversation
Transports — stdio for local/dev, Streamable HTTP for anything running as a shared service (which is what you'll run in production on AKS/Container Apps)
Capability negotiation — client and server exchange supported capabilities at connection time, so a runtime shouldn't assume every server supports every primitive

content.text: An 'agent manifest' is not yet a single universal industry standard the way a Kubernetes Deployment spec is, but the pattern that's converged across Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, and enterprise platform teams is a declarative document describing: the agent's identity/name/version, which model(s) it's allowed to call, which MCP servers/tools it's permitted to use (an allow-list, not implicit trust), runtime resource limits, and the identity it runs under. Standardizing this at the platform level is what lets you enforce 'agents can only call MCP servers explicitly declared in their manifest' as policy rather than convention.

content.code:
# Example agent manifest — platform-enforced, not just documentation
apiVersion: agents.adcb.internal/v1
kind: AgentManifest
metadata:
  name: txn-review-agent
  team: fraud-ops
spec:
  runtime:
    framework: langgraph
    image: acrbankprod.azurecr.io/agents/txn-review:1.4.0
    identity: workload-identity://txn-review-agent-sa
  model:
    provider: azure-ai-foundry
    deployment: gpt-4.1-prod
    maxTokens: 4096
  mcpServers:
    - name: policy-lookup
      endpoint: https://mcp-internal.adcb.local/policy-lookup
      allowedTools: ["get_policy", "list_policy_versions"]
    - name: case-management
      endpoint: https://mcp-internal.adcb.local/case-mgmt
      allowedTools: ["create_case"]
  limits:
    maxToolCallsPerTurn: 8
    timeoutSeconds: 30
  observability:
    tracing: otel
    logLevel: info

rows: stdio
Local dev, IDE-integrated tools
Not used in production platform — no network story, no scaling
Streamable HTTP (stateless, 2026 spec)
Production MCP servers behind a load balancer
Any pod/replica can serve any request — plays well with AKS/ACA horizontal scaling and rolling deploys
HTTP + SSE (legacy)
Older MCP servers, some third-party integrations
Requires sticky sessions or session affinity — a scaling and rolling-deploy complication to watch for

interviewQA.q: Explain MCP's architecture — host, client, server — and why that separation matters for a platform team.
interviewQA.a: The host is the application orchestrating the agent — say, a LangGraph process — and it holds one or more MCP clients, each a dedicated 1:1 connection to a single MCP server. The server is the thing that actually exposes tools, resources, and prompts. That separation matters to me as a platform engineer because it means I can deploy, scale, secure, and version MCP servers completely independently of the agents that consume them — a policy-lookup MCP server can be one shared, hardened service that ten different agents connect to, rather than each agent team reimplementing that integration and each getting the security wrong slightly differently.

interviewQA.q: What changed in the MCP spec's transport layer in 2026, and why does it matter operationally?
interviewQA.a: The July 2026 revision made the transport stateless — it removed the Mcp-Session-Id header and protocol-level sessions, so a request can be handled by any server instance rather than needing to stick to the instance that started the conversation. Operationally that's a big deal for us because it means MCP servers running behind a normal Kubernetes Service or Container Apps ingress with round-robin load balancing just work — I don't need sticky sessions, and rolling deployments don't risk killing an in-flight session on a specific pod. Older HTTP+SSE-based servers didn't have that property, so if I'm running one of those I need to plan for session affinity.

interviewQA.q: How would you enforce that an agent can only call the MCP tools it's supposed to, rather than trusting the agent code to behave?
interviewQA.a: I don't rely on the agent's own code to self-restrict — I enforce it at the manifest and gateway level. The agent manifest declares an explicit allow-list of MCP servers and even specific tool names it's permitted to use, and that manifest is what provisions the actual network policy and, ideally, an API gateway or service mesh authorization rule — so even if the agent code tried to call an undeclared tool, the network path simply wouldn't exist. That's the platform-engineering mindset: policy enforced as infrastructure, not as application-level good behavior.

interviewQA.q: Why doesn't a universal 'agent manifest' standard exist yet, and how do you deal with that as a platform team?
interviewQA.a: The space is moving too fast — Microsoft folded Semantic Kernel and AutoGen into Agent Framework in 2026, LangGraph and CrewAI have their own state and config models, and everyone's converging on similar concepts — model binding, tool allow-lists, resource limits — without a shared schema yet. My approach is to not wait for an external standard: I define our own internal agent manifest schema that captures the platform-relevant concerns — identity, allowed MCP servers, resource limits, observability config — regardless of which framework the team builds the agent logic in, and I keep the framework-specific bits (graph definitions, prompt chains) out of that manifest entirely. That way the platform's contract with application teams doesn't churn every time a framework has a major version change.

interviewQA.q: A team wants their agent to call an MCP server tool that reads directly from a core banking database. What do you push back on?
interviewQA.a: First question is whether that MCP tool is doing least-privilege reads — is it a narrowly scoped, parameterized query, or effectively 'run any SQL'? I'd insist the MCP server itself enforces a strict, reviewed set of callable operations rather than being a thin passthrough to the database, because the model's tool-selection isn't a security boundary I can trust. Second, I'd want that MCP server's identity to hold read-only, scoped database credentials via workload identity, not a shared service account, so a compromised or misbehaving agent can't escalate. And I'd want the interaction logged with enough fidelity — tool name, arguments, and result — to support an audit trail, since this is exactly the kind of access a bank's compliance team will ask about.

sections.heading: Secure Integration Patterns: Identity, Network, and Access Control for Agents
sections.summary: Covers how agents authenticate to models, MCP servers, and enterprise APIs using workload identity, private networking, and gateway-enforced access control — the security backbone of the whole runtime.

content.text: Azure AD Workload Identity is the standard, current (replacing the deprecated pod-managed identity approach) way pods authenticate to Azure services: a Kubernetes service account is federated to an Azure AD app registration or user-assigned managed identity via OIDC, so a pod exchanges its projected Kubernetes service account token for a short-lived Entra ID access token — no secrets stored in the cluster at all. The federated identity credential binds the exact subject `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account-name>`, so identity is scoped per workload, not shared across a team or namespace broadly. This is the pattern to describe when asked how an agent authenticates to Key Vault, a model endpoint, or a downstream enterprise API without embedding a client secret anywhere.

content.code:
# Kubernetes ServiceAccount federated to an Azure managed identity via Workload Identity
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: txn-review-agent-sa
  namespace: agents-prod
  annotations:
    azure.workload.identity/client-id: "3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6"
labels:
  azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
---
# Pod spec references the service account; no secrets mounted
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: txn-review-agent
  namespace: agents-prod
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: txn-review-agent-sa
      containers:
        - name: agent
          image: acrbankprod.azurecr.io/agents/txn-review:1.4.0

items: Agent to model: through Azure AI Foundry / APIM's AI Gateway tier, authenticated via workload identity, never a raw API key baked into a container image or config map
Agent to MCP server: private endpoint / internal VNet traffic only, with the MCP server itself validating the caller's identity token (not just 'anyone on the network can call me')

Agent to enterprise APIs: through APIM acting as the policy enforcement point — rate limiting, content-safety scanning of tool-call payloads, and audit logging of every call, per the AI Gateway capabilities Microsoft shipped through 2026
Secrets at rest: Azure Key Vault, mounted via the Secrets Store CSI driver so pods read files, not environment variables, and nothing is stored as a native Kubernetes Secret unless explicitly synced

Defense in depth: network policies restricting which namespaces/pods can reach which MCP servers, on top of identity-based auth — identity failing shouldn't be the only thing standing between an agent and a system it shouldn't touch

headers: Why it matters at a bank
rows: Agent → Key Vault
Secrets Store CSI driver + Workload Identity, secrets mounted as files
No plaintext secrets in env vars, images, or Kubernetes Secret objects; automatic rotation
Agent → LLM endpoint
Azure API Management AI Gateway tier fronting Foundry/Bedrock/Vertex
Single control point for content-safety policy, quota, and audit across every model call
Agent → MCP server
Private endpoint, mTLS or token-validated Streamable HTTP, tool allow-list per manifest
Prevents lateral movement and unauthorized tool use even if an agent is compromised
Agent → enterprise API
APIM with OAuth2 client-credentials via workload identity, not shared API keys
Traceable per-workload access for audit and incident response

interviewQA.q: Walk me through how a pod running an agent gets a token to call Azure Key Vault, without any secret being stored in the cluster.
interviewQA.a: The pod runs under a Kubernetes service account that's labeled for workload identity and annotated with the client ID of an Azure managed identity. When the pod starts, Kubernetes projects a signed service account token into the pod. The workload identity webhook injects environment variables and a token file path, and when the app's Azure SDK needs a token, it presents that Kubernetes token to Azure AD, which validates it against a federated identity credential — a trust relationship that says 'this specific service account in this specific namespace can impersonate this managed identity' — and issues a short-lived Entra ID access token in exchange. Nothing long-lived or secret ever lives in the cluster; it's pure OIDC federation, and the federated credential is scoped to one exact service account subject, so it's not a blanket trust.

interviewQA.q: How do you prevent an agent from using its legitimate MCP tool access to do something it shouldn't — like reading data outside its intended scope?
interviewQA.a: I stack three layers: the manifest-level allow-list restricts which MCP servers and tool names an agent can even attempt to call; the MCP server itself enforces least-privilege at the tool implementation level, so even an allowed tool can't return more than it's scoped to; and network policy plus workload identity ensures the agent's runtime identity has no path to the underlying data store except through that MCP server. None of these alone is sufficient — the manifest is just declared intent, the tool implementation can have bugs, and network policy alone doesn't stop an authorized call that's simply overreaching in scope — so the security property comes from all three being true simultaneously.

interviewQA.q: Why route agent-to-model traffic through an API gateway instead of calling Azure AI Foundry directly?
interviewQA.a: A gateway like APIM's AI Gateway tier gives me one place to enforce content-safety policy, quota and rate limiting per team, and consistent audit logging of every prompt and tool call across every agent in the bank, rather than each team's agent code independently deciding how to authenticate and log. It also lets me abstract away which underlying model provider is being used — APIM's unified model API can front Foundry, Bedrock, or Vertex behind one contract — so a team can be repointed to a different model without changing their agent code. For a regulated bank, having a single enforced checkpoint for what agents send and receive is close to non-negotiable from a compliance standpoint.

interviewQA.q: An application team wants to hardcode an API key for a third-party MCP server directly in their container image because 'it's faster.' How do you respond?
interviewQA.a: I'd explain why that's a hard no on the platform, not just a style preference — a key baked into an image ends up in every layer of every registry copy, in CI logs, and in anyone with pull access to the image, and it can't be rotated without a rebuild and redeploy. I'd offer the actual paved road instead: put the key in Key Vault, mount it via the Secrets Store CSI driver using their existing workload identity, and it's barely more setup than an env var, but it's rotatable, auditable, and never touches source control or image layers. If there's a genuine reason the paved road doesn't fit their case, I want to hear it — but in my experience it's almost always about not knowing the CSI driver path exists, not a real constraint.

interviewQA.q: How would you design network segmentation so a compromised agent in one team's namespace can't reach another team's MCP servers or data?
interviewQA.a: Default-deny network policies per namespace, with explicit allow rules only to the specific MCP server endpoints and APIs a given agent's manifest declares — so 'no implicit connectivity' is the baseline, not an afterthought. I'd back that with private endpoints for anything sensitive so traffic never traverses the public internet even accidentally, and where the blast radius justifies it, a service mesh with mTLS for cryptographic identity on every call, not just network-layer trust. The combination means even if an agent's code is compromised, its network reality is 'I can only reach exactly what I was provisioned to reach.'

sections.heading: Developer Self-Service: SDKs, Templates, and Onboarding Journeys
sections.summary: Covers how to make the platform actually usable — reference implementations, SDKs, and onboarding flows that get a team from zero to a deployed agent without recreating runtime decisions.

content.text: A platform nobody adopts is a platform that failed — industry data from 2026 puts developer adoption as the single biggest reason platform initiatives don't show impact. Self-service means an application team can go from an idea to a running, compliant agent without filing a ticket to the platform team for anything routine. That requires more than infrastructure: it requires a thin SDK/client library that wraps the platform's conventions (auth, MCP client setup, tracing) so teams don't reimplement boilerplate, a reference implementation (a real, working agent — not a toy hello-world) that teams can fork, and a documented onboarding journey with a clear entry point.

items: A lightweight internal SDK that pre-wires OpenTelemetry tracing, workload-identity token acquisition, and the standard MCP client configuration, so 'observable and secure by default' doesn't depend on each developer remembering to do it right
A Backstage (or equivalent internal developer portal) software template that scaffolds a new agent repo — code skeleton, Dockerfile, CI pipeline, Terraform call, and agent manifest — in one command

At least one production-grade reference implementation per major framework in use (e.g. a real LangGraph agent and a real Microsoft Agent Framework agent), since teams copy real code far more readily than they read docs

A staged onboarding journey: local dev with stdio MCP servers → shared dev/test environment → production promotion gated by the standard CI checks (security scan, policy-as-code checks, manifest validation)
Office hours / an internal Slack channel / a feedback loop, because self-service tooling still needs a human escape hatch for the 10% of cases that don't fit

content.code:
# What a strong onboarding journey looks like from the developer's side
$ agentctl new --template langgraph-agent --name claims-summarizer --team claims-ops
# scaffolds repo, Dockerfile, agent-manifest.yaml, GitHub Actions workflow

$ agentctl mcp add policy-lookup --scope claims-summarizer
# wires an MCP client connection + updates manifest allow-list + opens infra PR

$ git push origin main

interviewQA.q: How do you get busy application teams to actually adopt a self-service platform instead of building their own thing?
interviewQA.a: I make the paved road strictly faster than going around it — if using the platform SDK and templates saves a team real time in week one, adoption mostly takes care of itself; if it adds ceremony without visible benefit, they'll route around it no matter how good the guardrails are. Concretely that means investing in a genuinely good reference implementation and a scaffolding tool before asking anyone to use it, and treating the first two or three onboarding teams as design partners whose friction points get fixed immediately, not backlogged. I've also found that adoption follows a champion — get one respected team to build on the platform and succeed visibly, and others follow much faster than from a mandate.

interviewQA.q: What goes into an internal SDK for agent developers, and what do you deliberately leave out?
interviewQA.a: In: authentication and workload-identity token handling, MCP client setup against our standard server registry, OpenTelemetry tracing and structured logging wired in by default, and helpers for reading the agent manifest at runtime. Out: anything about the agent's actual reasoning logic, prompt design, or orchestration graph — that's squarely the application team's domain and framework choice, whether that's LangGraph, CrewAI, or Agent Framework. The SDK should be a thin, boring layer that makes the platform's non-negotiables (identity, observability, tool governance) automatic, and stay completely out of the way of how the team wants to build the actual agent.

interviewQA.q: Tell me about a time you had to convince a team to move off a bespoke solution onto a shared platform.
interviewQA.a: In a similar situation, the team's pushback wasn't really about the technology — it was that they'd already sunk weeks into their own deployment scripts and felt migrating would be pure cost with no benefit to them. I addressed that directly: I did the migration mapping myself, showed them line-by-line that their custom Terraform collapsed into a fifteen-line module call, and framed the win as 'you stop being on the hook for patching your own AKS ingress config when the next CVE lands' rather than 'please use our platform.' Once they saw the maintenance burden they were shedding, not just what they were gaining, they moved voluntarily — which is the outcome I want, because a mandated migration usually gets minimally-compliant effort and a resentful team.

interviewQA.q: How do you version a golden-path template without breaking every team already using an older version?
interviewQA.a: Templates and modules are semantically versioned and teams pin a version explicitly, so a breaking change to the template doesn't silently break existing deployments — it just means new scaffolds get the new version while existing repos stay put until they choose to upgrade. I publish a changelog and, for anything with security implications, actively reach out rather than waiting for teams to notice, but I don't force an upgrade outside of a security-driven deprecation window. The goal is that adopting the platform never feels like signing up for surprise breakage.

interviewQA.q: What's the difference between documentation and an onboarding journey, and why does that distinction matter?
interviewQA.a: Documentation is reference material someone reads when they already know what they're looking for; an onboarding journey is the guided, sequenced path that gets someone from zero context to a working deployment, with the right doc surfaced at the right moment rather than all at once. A wall of documentation with no journey just shifts the cognitive load back onto the developer to figure out what order to do things in, which defeats the purpose of a paved road. I design the journey first — scaffold, wire an MCP tool, deploy to dev, promote to prod — and then hang documentation off each concrete step rather than writing a standalone manual nobody reads end to end.

sections.heading: How to Talk About Your Experience: System Design and Behavioral Depth
sections.summary: Capstone section on framing your platform engineering background for this role and handling the broader system-design and behavioral questions interviewers use to test judgment under ambiguity.

content.text: This role sits at the intersection of platform engineering and emerging agent architecture, and most candidates over-index on one side. If you come from a pure Kubernetes/DevOps background, spend real prep time getting fluent in MCP's actual primitives and agent orchestration patterns (ReAct-style reasoning loops, tool-calling, multi-agent handoff) so you're not just describing infrastructure in the abstract. If you come from an AI/ML-adjacent background, spend the time on Terraform module design, workload identity federation mechanics, and platform-adoption thinking — because that's what this JD is actually weighted toward ('platform engineering first' is stated explicitly). When describing past experience, reframe any 'I built X service' story as 'I built a reusable pattern that N teams then used,' since that reuse multiplier is exactly what a bank's platform team is being funded to produce.

interviewQA.q: Design a secure, multi-tenant agent runtime platform for a bank from scratch. Walk me through your architecture.
interviewQA.a: I'd start from tenancy: each business unit gets its own Kubernetes namespace (or Container Apps environment) with default-deny network policy, its own workload-identity-bound service accounts, and its own Key Vault instance or vault path, so isolation is structural, not just RBAC convention. On top of that I'd put a platform API — Backstage templates plus Terraform modules — so a team provisions their agent workspace declaratively rather than a platform engineer clicking through the portal. Agents connect out to MCP servers over private endpoints only, governed by an agent manifest declaring an explicit tool allow-list, and all model and tool traffic routes through an API Management AI Gateway layer for content-safety policy, rate limiting, and audit logging in one place. Observability is OpenTelemetry-based and centralized so the platform team has cross-tenant visibility even though tenants can't see each other's data. And critically, I'd bake all of this into the paved-road module itself, so a team literally cannot provision a workload that skips workload identity or exposes a public MCP endpoint — the guardrail is the infrastructure, not a review step.

interviewQA.q: Tell me about a time you had to make a hard trade-off between developer velocity and security/compliance requirements.
interviewQA.a: In a prior platform role, a team wanted direct public ingress to a service to shave a few days off their timeline, and the security team's standard was everything routes through the API gateway. Instead of just enforcing the rule, I looked at why the gateway path felt slow to them — it turned out our gateway route provisioning was manual and took days, so I fixed the actual bottleneck by adding gateway route registration to the golden-path Terraform module, making the compliant path faster than the workaround. That's usually the resolution I look for: the trade-off is often a false choice created by the compliant path being badly engineered, not an inherent tension between security and speed.

interviewQA.q: Describe how you'd roll out a breaking change to a widely-used platform module — say, migrating from managed identity to workload identity federation — across dozens of teams.
interviewQA.a: I'd never do this as a single flag-day cutover. I'd ship the new pattern as a new module version, run both in parallel with the old one clearly marked deprecated with a sunset date, and provide a migration script or PR-bot that opens the diff automatically for consuming teams so it's a review-and-merge, not a rewrite. I'd communicate the deprecation timeline well in advance through whatever channel teams actually read — usually not just docs — and track migration progress on a dashboard so I know which teams need direct outreach as the sunset date approaches, rather than finding out on the deadline that half the fleet didn't move.

interviewQA.q: How do you approach observability for agent workloads specifically, versus a typical microservice?
interviewQA.a: Standard service metrics — latency, error rate, saturation — still matter, but agents need an additional layer: tracing the reasoning path itself, meaning which tools were called, in what order, with what arguments, and what the model's intermediate outputs were. I'd standardize on OpenTelemetry spans per tool call and per model call, correlated to a single trace per agent invocation, so when something goes wrong I can see not just 'the request failed' but 'the agent called the wrong tool because the manifest allow-list was misconfigured.' For a bank, I'd also keep this trace data as an audit artifact with defined retention, since 'what did the agent do and why' is a compliance question, not just a debugging convenience.

interviewQA.q: A team's agent workload has an incident in production — it's making unauthorized calls to an MCP tool outside its intended scope. Walk me through your response.
interviewQA.a: Immediate containment first: I'd pull the agent's workload identity's network policy or revoke the federated credential to cut its access path entirely, rather than trying to patch code under pressure. Then I'd pull the OTel traces and MCP server access logs to establish exactly what was called, with what arguments, and cross-reference against the agent manifest to determine whether this was a manifest misconfiguration, a gap in enforcement at the gateway, or an actual application bug generating unexpected tool calls. Once contained, the postmortem output has to be a platform fix, not just a fix to that one agent — if the manifest allow-list can be bypassed, that's a hole every other agent on the platform has too, so I'd prioritize closing the enforcement gap in the shared module over the individual incident.

interviewQA.q: Why do you want to work in an AI Center of Excellence at a bank specifically, rather than a pure product engineering role?
interviewQA.a: I like that the problem here is inherently cross-cutting — a CoE platform role means what I build gets multiplied across every team building agents, rather than shipping one team's feature. Banking specifically raises the stakes in a way I find genuinely interesting technically: the identity, audit, and access-control patterns aren't nice-to-haves, they're the actual hard engineering problem, which plays to what I care about most in platform work. And this space is moving fast enough — MCP's spec is still evolving, agent frameworks are still consolidating — that there's real architectural judgment to exercise here, not just executing an established playbook.
